extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of American political institutions / comparative local government
extracted.subtask_description: A descriptive account of the organization, types, functions, and practical working of local government in the United States (towns/townships, counties, and mixed systems), and of criteria bearing on admission of Territories as States. Emphasizes institutional roles, procedures, and historical causes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fitness for statehood / territorial admission
rubrics_metrics.description: A Territory should be fit for the rank of a self-governing State — having sufficient population, settled and stable communities, and adequate economic resources (cultivable soil, irrigation potential, ranching land, forests, mines) to support a large settled population.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author gives examples: the Dakotas (worthy because arable prairie and sufficient rain), Montana (large area but much uninhabitable mountain/forest; richer valleys and mines could support districts), Washington (moist coast, great forests), Utah (transformed by irrigation and Mormon settlement but delayed admission because of polygamy), Nevada (small, mining camps — example of a State whose scant population made admission imprudent). Warning: admitting small, unstable, or fluctuating mining populations risks political corruption (Nevada / 'rotten borough'). Also notes Congress has sometimes acted from party-political motives rather than strict fitness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constitutional rule on Federal suffrage for Territorial residents
rubrics_metrics.description: Under the Federal Constitution, only States choose representatives in Congress and Presidential electors; therefore territorial residents cannot be granted active Federal suffrage except by making the Territory a State.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains the legal/constitutional constraint: 'The Union is a union of States... The only means of granting Federal suffrage to citizens in a Territory was therefore to turn the Territory into a State.' This is offered as the reason territories lack congressional representation until statehood.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three regional types of rural local government
rubrics_metrics.description: There are three discernible types of rural local government: (1) the Town/Township system (New England), (2) the County-based system (Southern States), and (3) the Mixed system (Middle and North-western States).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each type is characterized by a different unit (town vs county) and by different political and social origins. The differences have practical consequences for representation, local participation, and administrative arrangements; the chapter aims to describe leading types and prominent features of each.

rubrics_metrics.name: Town (township) as local unit: size and meeting frequency
rubrics_metrics.description: The Town is the smallest rural local circumscription: area seldom exceeds five square miles; population usually small (often under 3,000, sometimes as low as under 200); governed by an assembly of all qualified voters which meets at least once a year (in the spring) and from time to time as summoned.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Notice for meetings is required at least ten days beforehand and must state hour, place, and the business to be brought forward. Meetings are usually three or four times a year; the town meeting is the central deliberative body.

rubrics_metrics.name: Town meeting powers and procedures
rubrics_metrics.description: The town assembly exercises both electoral and legislative powers: it elects selectmen and committees, enacts by-laws and ordinances, receives reports, passes accounts, votes taxation and appropriations for local purposes (schools, poor relief, highways), and manages town lands and property, including police and sanitation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Every resident has the right to propose and support proposals by speech; the meeting is presided over by a Moderator; meetings may be held in a town hall, church, schoolhouse or occasionally outdoors. The assembly's powers are compared to Roman Comitia and Swiss Landesgemeinde.

rubrics_metrics.name: Town executive officers and their roles
rubrics_metrics.description: The executive of a Town consists of selectmen (3–9, commonly 3, 5, or 7) elected annually who manage ordinary business under directions of the town meeting; there are also a town-clerk (records and registrar), a treasurer, assessors (valuation for taxation), a collector, school committee, and various minor officers (cemetery trustees, library trustees, field drivers/hog-reeves).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some officers are paid (selectmen usually), some unpaid (with expense reimbursement). The town-clerk typically keeps records and may register births and deaths. School committees sometimes have sub-committees for minor districts. Town elections are typically non-partisan in practice, though party spirit occasionally affects them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effective size and social composition for town-meeting democracy
rubrics_metrics.description: Town-meeting government works best when the electorate is not too large and is composed of citizens accustomed to local self-government (native stock); when numbers exceed about seven or eight hundred, or when many voters are recent immigrants or industrial operatives, deliberation becomes difficult and the institution may break down into faction and demagoguery.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author notes that town meetings of modest size produce sensible, practical debates and act as excellent schools of politics; they prevent jobbery and waste. But when attendance becomes very large or includes many untrained voters, the method ceases to function properly and can be captured by wirepullers or petty demagogues.

rubrics_metrics.name: The county as a judicial and administrative district
rubrics_metrics.description: The county is primarily a judicial district (aggregation of towns for judicial purposes) and a highway district; it holds civil and criminal courts, and certain judicial and county officers are elected by the people (including the sheriff and clerk).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The county's chief administrative officers are county commissioners (e.g., three in Massachusetts) and a county treasurer; commissioners manage county buildings (courthouses, prisons), may lay out inter-town highways, grant licences, estimate county taxation, and apportion the county tax among towns and cities. Police functions generally belong to towns and cities rather than to the county.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits on county authority and absence of county legislature
rubrics_metrics.description: County authorities are limited by statute to well-defined administrative functions; there is generally no county council or assembly with broad legislative functions, and the county has little power over towns except in specific statutory respects (e.g., taxation apportionment).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: county commissioners are controlled by the legislature; the county is 'in fact of small consequence' beyond judicial and highway functions. This contrasts with the broader legislative/administrative role towns can exercise via the town meeting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regional variation in importance of town vs county
rubrics_metrics.description: In New England the town is the primary political unit; in the Southern States the county is the original and principal unit; in the Middle and North-western States a mixed system emerges where the county may be the true unit in some places (NY, PA, OH) while townships remain vigorous and restrict county functions elsewhere.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These regional differences reflect original settlement patterns and social organization (Puritan town settlers in New England; plantation society in the South; mixed commercial and immigrant influences in the Middle States). The chapter links institutional form to historical causes and contemporary functions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Democratic implications of local-government forms
rubrics_metrics.description: The form of local government chosen has consequences for democratic education, local vigilance, and susceptibility to corruption: town systems tend to stimulate democratic habits and guard against jobbery, while county (Southern) systems were less democratic and less 'stimulating and educative'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author contrasts New England towns (miniature commonwealths exercising practical sovereignty and democratic habits) with Southern counties (semi-feudal estates, less urban life, authority concentrated among landowners), illustrating how social origins shape political effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of population mobility and occupational composition on territorial local institutions
rubrics_metrics.description: Populations drawn from transient pursuits (e.g., mining and ranching) are less likely to form stable, settled communities suitable for permanent local institutions; such fluctuating, disorderly populations make self-government and statehood less appropriate until settlement stabilizes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: mining populations in New Mexico and Arizona were described as fluctuating and disorderly; ranching and mining do not draw many permanent settlers. Thus the presence of a stable agricultural or diversified settled economy is a factor in readiness for fuller self-government/statehood.
